content: The Cambrian period is a geological time frame that began approximately 541 million years ago, marking the end of the Proterozoic Eon and the start of the Paleozoic Era within the Phanerozoic Eon. It concluded around 485 million years ago with the onset of the Ordovician period. The Cambrian is notable as the first period of the Paleozoic Era and derives its name from Cambria, the classical name for Wales, where rocks from this period were first studied. The Cambrian period is characterized by the presence of numerous large, multicellular organisms with hard body parts that fossilized well. This sudden emergence of diverse and fossilizable life forms is referred to as the Cambrian Explosion. The base of the Cambrian is defined by a specific assemblage of trace fossils known as the Trichophycus pedum assemblage, which includes vertically tiered burrows absent in older Precambrian rocks. This period was formally ratified internationally in 1994. The Cambrian is divided into three epochs: the Early Cambrian (Caerfai or Waucoban), the Middle Cambrian (St. Davids or Albertian), and the Furongian (Late Cambrian, also known as Merioneth or Croixan). Rocks from these epochs are classified as Lower, Middle, or Upper Cambrian, and each epoch is further subdivided into stages. However, only one stage, the Paibian, has been officially recognized by the International Commission on Stratigraphy, while others remain unnamed. Traditionally, the Cambrian was thought to span from 570 to 500 million years ago, with its lower boundary marked by the first appearance of trilobites and archaeocyathids, the latter being early sponges and the first non-microbial reef builders. The end of the Cambrian is defined by a significant faunal turnover, now recognized as an extinction event. Advances in fossil discoveries and radiometric dating in the late 20th century have refined these dates, with the Cambrian now estimated to span from approximately 541 to 485 million years ago. A notable carbon-13 isotope anomaly, or excursion, serves as a key marker for the Precambrian-Cambrian boundary, with evidence of this anomaly found in locations such as Oman, Siberia, and Namibia. During the Cambrian, the Earth's continents were shaped by the breakup of the Neoproterozoic supercontinent Pannotia. Gondwana remained the largest supercontinent, while Laurentia, Baltica, and Siberia existed as independent landmasses. The climate was significantly warmer than preceding glacial periods, with no polar glaciation. Shallow seas were widespread, and oceanic basins such as the Panthalassa, Proto-Tethys, Iapetus, and Khanty Oceans expanded during this time. The Cambrian fauna included representatives of nearly all modern animal phyla that fossilize easily, except for bryozoans. Many extinct phyla and enigmatic organisms with unclear evolutionary relationships also appeared. The rapid diversification of life forms during the Cambrian Explosion occurred over a relatively short geological timeframe. The first possible evidence of terrestrial tracks, such as Protichnites and Climactichnites, dating to around 530 million years ago, has been found in Ontario, Canada, and the northern United States. Conodonts, small predatory primitive chordates known from their fossilized teeth, also emerged during the Furongian epoch and thrived until their extinction in the Late Triassic. The Burgess Shale in British Columbia is one of the best-studied sites for Cambrian fossils, preserving soft-bodied organisms and providing critical insights into early animal diversity. Similar faunas have been discovered in other locations, such as the Maotianshan Shales in Yunnan Province, China. While extensive Precambrian Ediacaran faunas have been identified, their relationship to Cambrian forms remains unclear. Regarding flora, there is no evidence of land plants during the Cambrian, although molecular data suggests that land plant ancestors diverged from algae around 700 million years ago, and fungi diverged from animals approximately 1 billion years ago. The land during this period was barren, consisting mostly of deserts and badlands.
